analysis.one_liner: Extends a temporary tariff suspension on a synthetic musk fragrance chemical through 1998.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it sat in the Ways and Means trade subcommittee for about 18 months, and in September 1994 the record points to H.R. 5110 instead.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have kept a temporary import-duty suspension in place for one specific chemical, 7-acetyl-1,1,3,4,4,6-hexamethyltetrahydronaphthalene, through December 31, 1998 [S3]. That chemical is a synthetic musk used in fragrances and scented household products. The bill also would have let importers who paid the duty after the prior suspension lapsed at the end of 1992 apply to get that money back [S3]. The bill never got a vote; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its trade subcommittee in April 1993, stayed there, and on September 28, 1994 the record says "See H.R. 5110," meaning the tariff matter was being handled in that other bill [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that import or use this chemical — fragrance and household-product makers — would pay no import duty on it through 1998, and could claim refunds on duties paid after the end of 1992 [S3]. The savings are real but narrow, since they apply to a single specialty chemical rather than a broad class of goods.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends heading 9902.30.16 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule so that imports of the chemical face no duty through December 31, 1998 [S3].
It allows entries made between January 1, 1992 and shortly after enactment to be liquidated or reliquidated as if the suspension applied, refunding duties paid during the lapse [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury forgoes a small amount of tariff revenue on this one product, and any domestic producer of the same chemical loses a modest measure of tariff protection against imports [S3]. Consumers would barely notice either effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury and competing domestic producers, slightly

drawbacks.text: The suspension is a targeted break for a single product's importers rather than a general tax change, costing the Treasury a small amount of revenue with no broad benefit shown in the record [S3].
Removing the duty exposes whatever domestic production exists for this chemical to slightly cheaper imports, a cost its domestic competitors would bear [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes on both sides are tiny. Cheaper imported inputs could modestly lower costs for fragrance makers, while the Treasury loses a small stream of tariff revenue and any domestic producer of the chemical loses a little protection. There is no strong argument either way; the bill matters mostly as an example of a narrow trade measure that never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its trade subcommittee, request for and receipt of executive branch comments were noted, but no vote ever came; in September 1994 the record says to look to H.R. 5110 instead [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Gilman introduced the bill on March 31, 1993 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on March 31, 1993, and to the Subcommittee on Trade on April 2, 1993 [S5].
The committee requested comments from Treasury, Commerce, the International Trade Commission, and the U.S. Trade Representative in April 1993, and received a comment from the ITC in July 1993 [S5].
No further action occurred until September 28, 1994, when the record notes "See H.R. 5110," and the House never took an up-or-down vote on the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much from the bill dying. Because the prior suspension had lapsed at the end of 1992, importers of the chemical simply kept paying the small duty, and the Treasury kept collecting it; the outcome preserved the status quo rather than clearly favoring any side.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, collecting the small duty

for.role: House member, sponsor of the bill

against.what_they_did: Received the bill, sought executive-branch comments, and never scheduled it for consideration; it sat there for about 18 months until the record pointed to H.R. 5110.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors [S4], so no partisan split can be measured from the record; its sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Fragrance and household-product makers importing the chemical
industries.note: They would pay no import duty on this specialty chemical and could get refunds on duties paid after the 1992 lapse, lowering their input costs slightly. Ordinary consumers benefit only marginally, if at all, through cheaper inputs.

industries.industry: Domestic producers of the same chemical
industries.note: Extending the duty suspension exposes them to import competition without tariff protection. The effect is small given how narrow the product is.
The bill forgoes a small amount of customs revenue on one product line. The cost to the general public is negligible.
